title: 'Two Thanksgiving Day Gentlemen,' by O. Henry
english_text:
We present the short story "Two Thanksgiving Day Gentlemen," by O. Henry. The story was originally adapted and recorded by the U.S. Department of State.

There is one day that is ours. There is one day when all Americans go back to the old home and eat a big dinner. Bless the day. The President gives it to us every year.

Sometimes he talks about the people who had the first Thanksgiving. They were the Puritans. They were some people who landed on our Atlantic shore. We don’t really remember much about them.

But those people ate a large bird called turkey on the first Thanksgiving Day. So we have turkey for Thanksgiving dinner, if we have enough money to buy turkey. That is a tradition.

Yes. Thanksgiving Day is the one day of the year that is purely American. And now here is the story to prove to you that we have old traditions in this new country. They are growing older more quickly than traditions in old countries. That is because we are so young and full of life. We do everything quickly.

Stuffy Pete sat down on a seat in the New York City park named Union Square. It was the third seat to the right as you enter Union Square from the east.

Every Thanksgiving for nine years he had sat down there at one in the afternoon. Every time, things had happened to him. They were wonderful things. They made his heart feel full of joy—and they filled another part of him, too. They filled the part below his heart.

On those other Thanksgiving Days he had been hungry. (It is a strange thing. There are rich people who wish to help the poor. But many of them seem to think that the poor are hungry only on Thanksgiving Day.)

But today Pete was not hungry. He had come from a dinner so big that he had almost no power to move. His light green eyes looked out from a gray face on which there was still a little food. His breath was short. His body had suddenly become too big for his clothes; it seemed ready to break out of them. They were torn. You could see his skin through a hole in the front of his shirt. But the cold wind, with snow in it, felt pleasantly cool to him.

For Stuffy Pete was overheated with the warmth of all he had had to eat. The dinner had been much too big. It seemed to him that his dinner had included all the turkey and all the other food in the whole world.

So he sat, very, very full. He looked out at the world without interest, as if it could never offer him anything more.

The dinner had not been expected.

He had been passing a large house near the beginning of that great broad street called Fifth Avenue. It was the home of two old ladies of an old family. These two old ladies had a deep love of traditions. There were certain things they always did. On Thanksgiving Day at noon they always sent a servant to stand at the door. There he waited for the first hungry person who walked by. The servant had orders to bring that person into the house and feed him until he could eat no more. Stuffy Pete happened to pass by on his way to the park. The servant had gathered him in. Tradition had been followed.

Stuffy Pete sat in the park looking straight before him for ten minutes. Then he felt a desire to look in another direction. With a very great effort, he moved his head slowly to the left.

Then his eyes grew wider and his breath stopped. His feet in their torn shoes at the ends of his short legs moved about on the ground.

For the Old Gentleman was coming across Fourth Avenue toward Stuffy’s seat.

Every Thanksgiving Day for nine years the Old Gentleman had come there to find Stuffy Pete on his seat. That was a thing that the Old Gentleman was trying to make into a tradition. Every Thanksgiving Day for nine years he had found Stuffy there. Then he had led Stuffy to a restaurant and watched him eat a big dinner.

They do these things more easily in old countries like England. They do them without thinking about them.

But in this young country, we must think about them. In order to build a tradition, we must do the same thing again and again for a long time. The Old Gentleman loved his country. He believed he was helping to build a great American tradition. And he had been doing very well. Nine years is a long time here.

The Old Gentleman moved, straight and proud, toward the tradition that he was building. Truly feeding Stuffy Pete once a year was not a very important tradition. There are greater and more important traditions in England. But it was a beginning. It proved that a tradition was at least possible in America.

The Old Gentleman was thin and tall and sixty. He was dressed all in black. He wore eyeglasses. His hair was whiter and thinner than it had been last year. His legs did not seem as strong as they had seemed the year before.

As this kind Old Gentleman came toward him, Stuffy began to shake and his breath was shorter. He wished he could fly away. But he could not move from his seat.

“Good morning,” said the Old Gentleman. “I am glad to see that the troubles of another year have not hurt you. You continue to move in health about the beautiful world. For that blessing you and I can give thanks on this day of thanksgiving. If you will come with me, my man, I will give you a dinner that will surely make your body feel as thankful as your mind.”

That is what the Old Gentleman said every time. Every Thanksgiving Day for nine years. The words themselves were almost a tradition. Always before, they had been music in Stuffy’s ear. But now he looked up at the Old Gentleman’s face with tears of suffering in his eyes. The snow turned quickly to water when it fell upon his hot face. But the Old Gentleman was shaking with the cold. He turned away, with his back to the wind, and he did not see Stuffy’s eyes.

Stuffy had always wondered why the Old Gentleman seemed sad as he spoke. He did not know that it was because the Old Gentleman was wishing that he had a son. A son would come there after he himself was gone. A son would stand proud and strong before Stuffy, and say: “In remembrance of my father.” Then it would really be a tradition.

But the Old Gentleman had no family. He lived in a room in one of the old houses near the park. In the winter he grew a few flowers there. In the spring he walked on Fifth Avenue. In the summer he lived in a farmhouse in the hills outside New York, and he talked of a strange bug he hoped some day to find. In the fall season he gave Stuffy a dinner. These were the things that filled the Old Gentleman’s life.

Stuffy Pete looked up at him for a half minute, helpless and very sorry for himself. The Old Gentleman’s eyes were bright with the giving pleasure. His face was getting older every year, but his clothes were very clean and fresh.

And then Stuffy made a strange noise. He was trying to speak. As the Old Gentleman had heard the noise nine times before, he understood it. He knew that Stuffy was accepting.

“Thank you. I’m very hungry.”

Stuffy was very full, but he understood that he was part of a tradition. His desire for food on Thanksgiving Day was not his own. It belonged to this kind Old Gentleman. True, America is free. But there are some things that must be done.

The Old Gentleman led Stuffy to the restaurant and to the same table where they had always gone. They were known here.

“Here comes that old man,” said a waiter, “that buys that old no-good fellow a dinner every Thanksgiving.”

The Old Gentleman sat at the table, watching. The waiters brought food, and more food. And Stuffy began to eat.

No great and famous soldier ever battled more strongly against an enemy. The turkey and all the other food were gone almost as quickly as they appeared. Stuffy saw the look of happiness on the Old Gentleman’s face. He continued to eat in order to keep it there.

In an hour the battle was finished.

“Thank you,” Stuffy said. “Thank you for my Thanksgiving dinner.” Then he stood up heavily and started to go to the wrong door. A waiter turned him in the right direction.

The Old Gentleman carefully counted out $1.30, and left fifteen cents more for the waiter.

They said goodbye, as they did each year, at the door. The Old Gentleman went south, and Stuffy went north.

Stuffy went around the first corner, and stood for one minute. Then he fell.

There he was found. He was picked up and taken to a hospital. They put him on a bed, and began to try to discover what strange sickness had made him fall.

And an hour later the Old Gentleman was brought to the same hospital. And they put him on another bed, and began to try to discover what his sickness could be.

After a little time one of the doctors met another doctor, and they talked.

“That nice old gentleman over there,” he said. “Do you know what’s wrong with him? He’s almost dead for the need of food. A very proud old man, I think. He told me he has had nothing to eat for three days.”

我们呈现欧·亨利的短篇小说《两位感恩节的绅士》。该故事最初由美国国务院改编并录制。

有一个日子是属于我们的。有一个日子，所有美国人回到老家，吃一顿丰盛的晚餐。祝福这个日子吧。总统每年把它赐给我们。

有时他会谈起那些度过第一个感恩节的人。他们是清教徒。他们是一群登上我们大西洋海岸的人。我们其实对他们记得不多。

但那些人在第一个感恩节吃了一种叫做火鸡的大鸟。所以，如果我们有足够的钱买火鸡，我们的感恩节晚餐就吃火鸡。那是一种传统。

是的。感恩节是一年中纯粹属于美国的日子。现在这里有一个故事，向你证明我们在这个新国家也有古老的传统。它们比老国家的传统老得更快。那是因为我们如此年轻、充满活力。我们做一切事情都很快。

斯塔菲·皮特坐在纽约市联合广场公园的一条长椅上。那是从东边进入联合广场后右手边的第三条长椅。

九年来，每个感恩节的下午一点他都坐在那里。每次，总有些事情发生在他身上。那些都是奇妙的事。它们让他心里充满喜悦——也填充了他身体的另一部分。它们填满了他心脏下方的部分。

在过去的那些感恩节，他总是饥肠辘辘。（这是一件奇怪的事。有些富人想要帮助穷人。但他们中的许多人似乎认为穷人只在感恩节那天挨饿。）

但今天皮特并不饿。他刚刚吃了一顿大餐，大到他几乎没有力气动弹。他那浅绿色的眼睛从一张灰色的脸上望出来，脸上还沾着一点食物。他呼吸短促。他的身体突然变得太大，撑得衣服快要裂开；似乎随时会撑破它们。衣服都撕裂了。透过衬衫前面的一个洞，你能看到他的皮肤。但夹着雪的寒风，却让他感到惬意的凉爽。

因为斯塔菲·皮特吃了太多东西，身上热得厉害。那顿饭实在太过丰盛。在他看来，他的这顿饭包含了全世界所有的火鸡和其他食物。

于是他坐在那里，撑得不能再撑。他毫无兴趣地望着外面的世界，仿佛这个世界再也给不了他任何东西。

这顿饭本不是他预料之中的。

他刚才经过一栋大房子，它靠近那条宽阔的大街——第五大道的起点处。那是古老家族两位老太太的家。这两位老太太深爱传统。有些事情她们总是会做。感恩节中午，她们总是派一名仆人在门口站着。仆人在那里等待第一个经过的饥饿的人。仆人接到命令，要把那个人带进屋里，喂到他再也吃不下为止。斯塔菲·皮特在去公园的路上恰好经过。仆人将他收了进去。传统得到了遵循。

斯塔菲·皮特坐在公园里，直视前方十分钟。然后他想看看另一个方向。他费了很大的劲，慢慢地把头转向左边。

然后他瞪大了眼睛，屏住了呼吸。他那两条短腿末端穿着破鞋的双脚在地上挪动起来。

因为那位老绅士正穿过第四大街朝斯塔菲的座位走来。

九年来，每个感恩节，老绅士都会来到这里，在斯塔菲的长椅上找到他。那是老绅士想要把它变成一种传统的事情。九年来，每个感恩节他都会在那儿找到斯塔菲。然后他会带斯塔菲去一家餐馆，看着他吃一顿大餐。

在像英格兰这样的老国家，人们做这些事情更轻松自然。他们做这些事情时想都不用想。

但是在这个年轻的国家里，我们必须考虑这些。为了建立一种传统，我们必须长时间地一次又一次地做同一件事。老绅士热爱他的国家。他相信自己正在帮助建立一项伟大的美国传统。而且他一直做得很好。九年在这里是一段很长的时间。

老绅士挺直而自豪地走向他正在建立的传统。每年喂饱斯塔菲·皮特一次确实算不上什么重要的传统。英国有更伟大、更重要的传统。但这是一个开始。它证明了在美国至少有可能建立一种传统。

老绅士又瘦又高，六十岁了。他全身穿着黑衣。他戴着眼镜。他的头发比去年更白、更稀疏了。他的腿似乎也不如去年那么结实了。

当这位仁慈的老绅士向他走来时，斯塔菲开始发抖，呼吸变得更加短促。他希望自己能飞走。但他无法从座位上移动。

“早上好，”老绅士说。“我很高兴看到又一年的烦恼没有伤害到你。你继续健康地行走在这美丽的世界中。为了这一福分，你和我可以在这个感恩的日子里表示感谢。如果你愿意跟我来，我的伙计，我会给你一顿饭，它必定会让你的身体和你的心灵一样充满感激。”

这就是老绅士每次说的话。九年来的每一个感恩节都是如此。这些话本身几乎成了一种传统。以往每一次，它们都是斯塔菲耳中的音乐。但现在他抬头看着老绅士的脸，眼中满含痛苦的泪水。雪花落在他滚烫的脸上，立刻化成了水。但老绅士正冷得发抖。他转过身去，背对着风，没有看到斯塔菲的眼睛。

斯塔菲一直想知道，为什么老绅士说话时似乎带着忧伤。他不知道那是因为老绅士希望自己有一个儿子。等他去世之后，会有一个儿子来到这里。那个儿子会骄傲而强壮地站在斯塔菲面前，说道：“纪念我的父亲。”那样这才会真正成为一项传统。

但老绅士没有家人。他住在公园附近一栋老房子里的一间屋子里。冬天他在那里种一些花。春天他在第五大道上散步。夏天他住在纽约城外山中的一座农舍里，谈论着一种他希望有一天能找到的奇异虫子。秋天他请斯塔菲吃一顿饭。这些就是填满老绅士生活的事情。

斯塔菲·皮特抬头看了他半分钟，无可奈何，也为自己深感难过。老绅士的眼中闪烁着给予的快乐。他的脸一年比一年苍老，但他的衣服非常干净整洁。

然后斯塔菲发出了一声奇怪的声响。他在努力说话。由于老绅士之前已经听过这声音九次，他明白它的意思。他知道斯塔菲是在接受。

“谢谢你。我真的很饿。”

斯塔菲很饱，但他明白自己是一项传统的一部分。他在感恩节对食物的渴望并不是他自己的。它属于这位仁慈的老绅士。的确，美国是自由的。但有些事情是必须做的。

老绅士带着斯塔菲去了那家餐馆，来到他们一直坐的那张桌子前。他们在这里是熟面孔。

“那个老头来了，”一个侍者说，“就是那个每年感恩节给那个没用的家伙买一顿饭的人。”

老绅士坐在桌边，看着。侍者们端来食物，更多的食物。斯塔菲开始吃了起来。

没有哪位伟大而著名的士兵与敌人进行过更顽强的战斗。火鸡和所有其他食物几乎一出现就被消灭了。斯塔菲看到了老绅士脸上幸福的神情。他继续吃着，以保持那神情留在那里。

一个小时过后，战斗结束了。

“谢谢你，”斯塔菲说。“谢谢你给我这顿感恩节晚餐。”然后他沉重地站起身来，朝错误的门口走去。一位侍者把他转向了正确的方向。

老先生仔细数出一美元三十美分，又留下十五美分给侍者作为小费。

和每年一样，他们在门口道别。老先生往南走，斯塔菲往北走。

斯塔菲绕过第一个街角，站了一分钟。然后他倒了下去。

他就在那里被发现了。他被扶起来，送进了一家医院。他们把他放到一张床上，开始尝试查明是什么奇怪的疾病让他倒下的。

一小时后，老先生也被送到了同一家医院。他们把他放到另一张床上，开始尝试查明他得的是什么病。

过了一会儿，一位医生遇到了另一位医生，他们交谈起来。

“那边那位可敬的老先生，”他说。“您知道他得了什么病吗？他饿得快死了。我想，是一位非常自尊的老人。他告诉我他已经三天没吃过任何东西了。”

english_text:
Our story today is called "The Purloined Letter." It was written by Edgar Allan Poe. Poe is generally known for his horror stories. This is the third of three stories he wrote about Auguste Dupin and how he solves crimes. The story is about a stolen letter. It first appeared in 1844 in a yearly magazine. It was reprinted in many publications, newspapers and books. This is one of Poe's stories that influenced the development of the modern detective story.

One evening in Paris, during the autumn of eighteen forty-five, I went to visit a friend, Auguste Dupin. We were smoking our pipes and talking when the door of his apartment opened. Mr. Germont, the head of the Paris police force, came into the room.

"I came to ask your advice," Germont said to my friend Dupin. "I am trying to solve a very important case. It is also a very simple case, so I really need your help. But I thought you would like to hear about it, because it is so strange.

"My men and I have worked on this case for three months," Germont said. "It is a very simple case of robbery. But we still cannot solve it."

Dupin took the pipe out of his mouth. "Perhaps the mystery is too simple," he said.

Germont began to laugh. "Too simple?" he said. "Who ever heard of such a thing?"

I looked at Germont. "Why don't you tell us the problem?" I said.

Germont stopped laughing and sat down.

"All right," he said. "But you must never tell anyone I told you this."

"The wife of a very important person needs help. I cannot tell you her name, because her husband is a powerful man in the French government. Let us just call her Madame X. Three months ago, someone stole a letter from Madame X. She is offering a large amount of money to anyone who can return the letter to her.

"We know that her husband's political enemy, Mr. D'Arcy, stole the letter. We also know it is somewhere in his apartment. D'Arcy plans to use the letter to embarrass Madame X's husband and destroy his political power.

"As you know, I have keys which can open any lock in Paris. For the last three months, my men and I have spent every evening looking for the letter in his apartment. But we cannot find it."

Dupin stopped smoking. "Tell me how you looked for it," he said. Germont moved forward in his chair.

"We took our time," he said. "First, we examined the furniture in every room. We opened all the drawers. We looked under the rugs. We searched behind all the paintings on the walls.

"We opened every book. We removed the boards of the floor. We even took the tops off the tables to see if he had hidden the letter in the table legs. But we cannot find it. What do you advise me to do?"

Dupin puffed on his pipe. "What does the letter look like?" he asked.

"It is in a white envelope with a red stamp," Germont said. "The address is written in large black letters."

Dupin puffed on his pipe again. "I advise you to go back and search the apartment again," he said.

About one month later, Germont came back to see us.

"I followed your advice," he said. "But I still have not found the letter."

Dupin smiled. "I knew you would not find it," he said. Germont became very red in the face. "Then why did you make me search the apartment again?" he shouted.

"My dear Germont," Dupin said. "Let me tell you a little story. Do you remember the famous doctor, Louis Abernathy?"

"No!" Germont shouted. "Get to the point, Dupin!"

"Of course! Of course," Dupin said. "Once, a rich old man met Abernathy at a party. The old man was not feeling very well. He decided he would get a medical opinion from the doctor without paying for it. So he described his problems to Abernathy. 'Now doctor,' the old man said, 'suppose you had a patient like that. What would you tell him to take?'"

"'Oh, that is quite simple,' said Abernathy. 'I would tell him to take my advice.'"

Germont looked embarrassed. "Look here, Dupin. I am perfectly willing to pay for advice."

Dupin smiled at Germont. "How much money did you say the reward was?" he asked. Germont sighed. "I do not want to tell you the exact amount. But I would give fifty thousand francs to the person who helps me find that letter."

"In that case," Dupin said, "take out your checkbook and write me a check for fifty thousand francs. When you have signed the check, I will give you the letter."

Germont looked at Dupin with his mouth open. His eyes seemed to jump out of his head. Then he took out his checkbook and pen, and wrote a check for fifty thousand francs. He gave it to Dupin.

My friend examined the check carefully and put it in his pocket. Then he unlocked a drawer of his desk, took out the letter, and gave it to Germont.

The policeman's hands shook as he opened the letter. He read it quickly. Then he put it in his pocket and ran out of the room without saying a word.

"Dupin!" I said, as I turned to my friend. "How did you solve the mystery?"

"It was simple, my friend," he said. "Germont and his policemen could not find the letter, because they did not try to understand the mind of the man who stole it. Instead, they looked for the letter where they would have hidden it.

"Mr. D'Arcy is not a policeman. He is, however, very intelligent. He knew the police would search his apartment. He also knew how police think. So, he did not hide the letter where he knew they would look for it.

"Do you remember how Germont laughed when I said the mystery was difficult for him to solve because it was so simple?"

Dupin filled his pipe with tobacco and lit it. "Well, the more I thought about it, the more I realized the police could not find the letter because D'Arcy had not hidden it at all.

"So I went to visit D'Arcy in his apartment. I took a pair of dark green eyeglasses with me. I explained to him that I was having trouble with my eyes and needed to wear the dark glasses at all times. He believed me. The glasses permitted me to look around the apartment while I seemed only to be talking to him.

"I paid special attention to a large desk where there were a lot of papers and books. However, I saw nothing suspicious there. After a few minutes, however, I noticed a small shelf over the fireplace. A few postcards and a letter were lying on the shelf. The letter looked very old and dirty.

"As soon as I saw this letter, I decided it must be the one I was looking for. It must be, even though it was completely different from the one Germont had described.

"This letter had a large green stamp on it. The address was written in small letters in blue ink. I memorized every detail of the letter while I talked to D'Arcy. Then when he was not looking, I dropped one of my gloves on the floor under my chair.

"The next morning, I stopped at his apartment to look for my glove. While we were talking, we heard people shouting in the street. D'Arcy went to the window and looked out. Quickly, I stepped to the shelf and put the letter in my pocket. Then I replaced it with a letter that looked exactly like it, which I had taken with me. I had made it the night before.

"The trouble in the street was caused by a man who had almost been run over by a horse and carriage. He was not hurt. And soon the crowd of people went away. When it was over, D'Arcy came away from the window. I said good-bye and left.

"The man who almost had an accident was one of my servants. I had paid him to create the incident."

Dupin stopped talking to light his pipe. I did not understand. "But, Dupin," I said, "why did you go to the trouble of replacing the letter? Why not just take it and leave?"

Dupin smiled. "D'Arcy is a dangerous man," he said. "And he has many loyal servants. If I had taken the letter, I might never have left his apartment alive."

The Purloined Letter was written by Edgar Allan Poe and adapted by Dona De Sanctis. The storyteller was Shep O'Neal. The producer was Lawan Davis.

我们今天的故事叫做《失窃的信》。它由埃德加·爱伦·坡创作。坡通常以其恐怖故事而闻名。这是他所写的关于奥古斯特·杜宾如何侦破罪案的三篇小说中的第三篇。这个故事讲的是一封被偷的信。它于1844年首次出现在一份年刊杂志上。后来被许多出版物、报纸和书籍转载。这是坡影响现代侦探故事发展的作品之一。

一八四五年秋天的一个晚上，在巴黎，我去拜访一位朋友，奥古斯特·杜宾。我们正在抽着烟斗聊天，这时他公寓的门开了。巴黎警察局局长热尔蒙先生走进了房间。

“我是来向你请教的，”热尔蒙对我的朋友杜宾说。“我正在侦办一件非常重要的案子。这个案子也很简单，所以我确实需要你的帮助。但我想你也会愿意听听，因为它很奇怪。”

“我和我的手下已经对此案调查了三个月，”热尔蒙说。“这是一宗非常简单的盗窃案。但我们仍然无法破案。”

杜宾把烟斗从嘴里拿出来。“也许这个谜团过于简单了，”他说。

热尔蒙开始大笑。“过于简单？”他说，“谁听说过这种事？”

我看着热尔蒙。“你为什么不把问题告诉我们呢？”我说。

热尔蒙停止了大笑，坐了下来。

“好吧，”他说。“但你绝不能告诉任何人这是我告诉你的。”

“一位非常重要人物的妻子需要帮助。我不能告诉你们她的名字，因为她的丈夫在法国政府中是一位有权势的人物。我们就称她为X夫人吧。三个月前，有人偷走了X夫人一封信。她正在向任何能将信归还给她的人提供一大笔钱。”

“我们知道是她丈夫的政治对手达西先生偷了那封信。我们也知道信就在他的公寓里某个地方。达西计划利用这封信让X夫人的丈夫难堪，并摧毁他的政治权力。”

“正如你所知，我有能打开巴黎任何锁的钥匙。在过去的三个月里，我和我的手下每天晚上都在他的公寓里寻找那封信。但我们找不到它。”

杜宾停止了吸烟。“告诉我你们是怎么找的，”他说。热尔蒙在椅子上向前倾身。

“我们花了时间仔细搜查，”他说。“首先，我们检查了每个房间的家具。我们打开了所有抽屉。我们查看了地毯下面。我们搜查了墙上所有画作的后面。”

“我们打开了每一本书。我们拆下了地板。我们甚至掀开了桌面，看看他有没有把信藏在桌腿里。但我们找不到它。你有什么建议？”

杜宾抽了一口烟斗。“那封信是什么样子的？”他问道。

“它在白色信封里，上面有一枚红色邮票，”热尔蒙说。“地址是用大大的黑色字体写的。”

杜宾又抽了一口烟斗。“我建议你们回去再搜查一次那间公寓，”他说。

大约一个月后，热尔蒙回来看我们。

“我听从了你的建议，”他说。“但我仍然没有找到那封信。”

杜宾微笑了。“我知道你们找不到它，”他说。热尔蒙的脸涨得通红。“那你为什么还要让我再去搜查那间公寓？”他喊道。

“亲爱的热尔蒙，”杜宾说，“让我给你讲一个小故事。你还记得那位著名的医生路易·阿伯内西吗？”

“不记得！”热尔蒙喊道。“说重点，杜宾！”

“当然！当然，”杜宾说。“有一次，一位富有的老人在聚会上遇见了阿伯内西。老人感觉不太舒服。他决定从医生那里得到医疗意见，但不想付钱。于是他把自己的问题描述给阿伯内西听。‘那么医生，’老人说，‘假设你有一个这样的病人。你会告诉他吃什么药？’”

“‘哦，那很简单，’阿伯内西说，‘我会告诉他接受我的建议。’”

热尔蒙看起来很难为情。“听我说，杜宾。我非常愿意为建议付钱。”

杜平朝热尔蒙微笑着说：“你说赏金有多少来着？”热尔蒙叹了口气。“我不想告诉你确切数额。但谁要是帮我找到那封信，我愿意给他五万法郎。”

“这样的话，”杜平说，“拿出你的支票簿，给我开一张五万法郎的支票。你签好支票，我就把信给你。”

热尔蒙张着嘴看着杜平。他的眼睛似乎要从眼眶里跳出来。然后他拿出支票簿和笔，开了一张五万法郎的支票。他把支票递给杜平。

我的朋友仔细检查了支票，把它放进口袋。然后他打开写字台的抽屉，取出那封信，递给热尔蒙。

警长打开信时，双手发抖。他飞快地读了一遍。然后把信放进口袋，一句话也没说就跑出了房间。

“杜平！”我转过身对朋友说。“你是怎么解开这个谜的？”

“很简单，我的朋友，”他说。“热尔蒙和他的警察们找不到那封信，是因为他们没有试着去理解偷信人的心思。他们只是在换作他们会藏信的地方找信。

“达西先生不是警察。但他非常聪明。他知道警察会搜查他的公寓。他也知道警察是怎么想的。所以，他没有把信藏在他知道警察会去找的地方。

“你还记得我说这个谜对他来说难解是因为它太简单时，热尔蒙是怎么笑的吗？”

杜平往烟斗里装满了烟草，点燃了它。“嗯，我越想越觉得，警察找不到信，是因为达西根本没有把信藏起来。

“于是我去达西的公寓拜访他。我带了一副深绿色眼镜。我向他解释说我的眼睛有毛病，需要一直戴着这副深色眼镜。他相信了。这副眼镜让我可以在看似只是在和他说话的同时，打量他的公寓。

“我特别留意了一张大写字台，上面堆着许多纸张和书籍。但我在那里没看到任何可疑的东西。不过，几分钟后，我注意到壁炉上方有一个小架子。架子上放着几张明信片和一封信。那封信看起来很旧很脏。

“我一看到这封信，就断定它一定是我要找的那一封。一定是它，尽管它和热尔蒙描述的那封信完全不同。

“这封信上贴着一张大的绿色邮票。地址是用蓝色墨水写的小字。我和达西说话的时候，把信的每一个细节都记在心里。然后趁他不注意，我把一只手套掉在椅子下面的地板上。

“第二天早上，我顺路去他的公寓找我的手套。我们正说着话，听到街上有人喊叫。达西走到窗边往外看。我迅速走到架子前，把信放进口袋。然后我用一封我随身带来的、看起来一模一样的信替换了它。那封信是我头天晚上做好的。

“街上的骚乱是一个差点被马车撞倒的人引起的。他没有受伤。很快那群人就散了。事情结束后，达西从窗边走了回来。我说了声再见就离开了。

“那个差点出事的人是我的一个仆人。我花钱让他制造了那场意外。”

杜平停下来点烟斗。我不明白。“但是，杜平，”我说，“你为什么费那么大劲去替换那封信呢？为什么不直接拿走信然后离开？”

杜平笑了笑。“达西是个危险的人，”他说。“而且他有许多忠心耿耿的仆人。如果我当时直接拿走信，我可能就没命活着离开他的公寓了。”

《被偷窃的信》由埃德加·爱伦·坡创作，多娜·德·桑克蒂斯改编。讲述者谢普·奥尼尔。制作人拉万·戴维斯。

测验——《失窃的信》埃德加·爱伦·坡

title: 'The Tell-Tale Heart' by Edgar Allan Poe
english_text:
Today we present the short story "The Tell-Tale Heart" by Edgar Allan Poe. Here is Shep O'Neal with the story.

True! Nervous -- very, very nervous I had been and am! But why will you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses -- not destroyed them.

Above all was the sense of hearing. I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in the underworld. How, then, am I mad? Observe how healthily -- how calmly I can tell you the whole story.

It is impossible to say how first the idea entered my brain. I loved the old man. He had never wronged me. He had never given me insult. For his gold I had no desire. I think it was his eye! Yes, it was this! He had the eye of a bird, a vulture -- a pale blue eye, with a film over it. Whenever it fell on me, my blood ran cold; and so -- very slowly -- I made up my mind to take the life of the old man, and free myself of the eye forever.

Now this is the point. You think that I am mad. Madmen know nothing. But you should have seen me. You should have seen how wisely and carefully I went to work!

I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I killed him. And every night, late at night, I turned the lock of his door and opened it – oh, so gently! And then, when I had made an opening big enough for my head, I put in a dark lantern, all closed that no light shone out, and then I stuck in my head. I moved it slowly, very slowly, so that I might not interfere with the old man's sleep. And then, when my head was well in the room, I undid the lantern just so much that a single thin ray of light fell upon the vulture eye.

And this I did for seven long nights -- but I found the eye always closed; and so it was impossible to do the work; for it was not the old man who was a problem for me, but his Evil Eye.

On the eighth night, I was more than usually careful in opening the door. I had my head in and was about to open the lantern, when my finger slid on a piece of metal and made a noise. The old man sat up in bed, crying out "Who's there?"

I kept still and said nothing. I did not move a muscle for a whole hour. During that time, I did not hear him lie down. He was still sitting up in the bed listening -- just as I have done, night after night.

Then I heard a noise, and I knew it was the sound of human terror. It was the low sound that arises from the bottom of the soul. I knew the sound well. Many a night, late at night, when all the world slept, it has welled up from deep within my own chest. I say I knew it well.

I knew what the old man felt, and felt sorry for him, although I laughed to myself. I knew that he had been lying awake ever since the first noise, when he had turned in the bed. His fears had been ever since growing upon him.

When I had waited a long time, without hearing him lie down, I decided to open a little -- a very, very little -- crack in the lantern. So I opened it. You cannot imagine how carefully, carefully. Finally, a single ray of light shot from out and fell full upon the vulture eye.

It was open -- wide, wide open -- and I grew angry as I looked at it. I saw it clearly -- all a dull blue, with a horrible veil over it that chilled my bones; but I could see nothing else of the old man's face or person. For I had directed the light exactly upon the damned spot.

And have I not told you that what you mistake for madness is but a kind of over-sensitivity? Now, there came to my ears a low, dull, quick sound, such as a watch makes when inside a piece of cotton. I knew that sound well, too. It was the beating of the old man's heart. It increased my anger.

But even yet I kept still. I hardly breathed. I held the lantern motionless. I attempted to keep the ray of light upon the eye. But the beating of the heart increased. It grew quicker and quicker, and louder and louder every second. The old man's terror must have been extreme! The beating grew louder, I say, louder every moment!

And now at the dead hour of the night, in the horrible silence of that old house, so strange a noise as this excited me to uncontrollable terror. Yet, for some minutes longer I stood still. But the beating grew louder, louder! I thought the heart must burst.

And now a new fear seized me -- the sound would be heard by a neighbor! The old man's hour had come! With a loud shout, I threw open the lantern and burst into the room.

He cried once -- once only. Without delay, I forced him to the floor, and pulled the heavy bed over him. I then smiled, to find the action so far done.

But, for many minutes, the heart beat on with a quiet sound. This, however, did not concern me; it would not be heard through the wall. At length, it stopped. The old man was dead. I removed the bed and examined the body. I placed my hand over his heart and held it there many minutes. There was no movement. He was stone dead. His eye would trouble me no more.

If still you think me mad, you will think so no longer when I describe the wise steps I took for hiding the body. I worked quickly, but in silence. First of all, I took apart the body. I cut off the head and the arms and the legs.

I then took up three pieces of wood from the flooring, and placed his body parts under the room. I then replaced the wooden boards so well that no human eye -- not even his -- could have seen anything wrong.

There was nothing to wash out -- no mark of any kind -- no blood whatever. I had been too smart for that. A tub had caught all -- ha! ha!

When I had made an end of these labors, it was four o'clock in the morning. As a clock sounded the hour, there came a noise at the street door. I went down to open it with a light heart -- for what had I now to fear? There entered three men, who said they were officers of the police. A cry had been heard by a neighbor during the night; suspicion of a crime had been aroused; information had been given at the police office, and the officers had been sent to search the building.

I smiled -- for what had I to fear? The cry, I said, was my own in a dream. The old man, I said, was not in the country. I took my visitors all over the house. I told them to search -- search well. I led them, at length, to his room. I brought chairs there, and told them to rest. I placed my own seat upon the very place under which lay the body of the victim.

The officers were satisfied. I was completely at ease. They sat, and while I answered happily, they talked of common things. But, after a while, I felt myself getting weak and wished them gone. My head hurt, and I had a ringing in my ears; but still they sat and talked.

The ringing became more severe. I talked more freely to do away with the feeling. But it continued until, at length, I found that the noise was not within my ears.

I talked more and with a heightened voice. Yet the sound increased -- and what could I do? It was a low, dull, quick sound like a watch makes when inside a piece of cotton. I had trouble breathing -- and yet the officers heard it not. I talked more quickly -- more loudly; but the noise increased. I stood up and argued about silly things, in a high voice and with violent hand movements. But the noise kept increasing.

Why would they not be gone? I walked across the floor with heavy steps, as if excited to anger by the observations of the men -- but the noise increased. What could I do? I swung my chair and moved it upon the floor, but the noise continually increased. It grew louder -- louder -- louder! And still the men talked pleasantly, and smiled.

Was it possible they heard not? No, no! They heard! They suspected! They knew! They were making a joke of my horror! This I thought, and this I think. But anything was better than this pain! I could bear those smiles no longer! I felt that I must scream or die! And now -- again! Louder! Louder! Louder!

"Villains!" I cried, "Pretend no more! I admit the deed! Tear up the floor boards! Here, here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!"

今天我们为大家介绍埃德加·爱伦·坡的短篇小说《泄密的心》。下面由谢普·奥尼尔为大家讲述这个故事。

不错！我紧张——非常非常紧张，过去和现在都是如此！可你们为什么说我疯了呢？这种病让我的感官变得敏锐——并没有摧毁它们。

尤其是听觉。我能听见天上和地上的一切。我能听见冥界里的许多事情。那么，我怎么会疯呢？看看我多么健康——多么平静地讲述整个故事吧。

很难说这个念头最初是怎么钻进我脑子里的。我爱那位老人。他从未亏待过我，从未侮辱过我。对他的金子我毫无贪念。我想是他的眼睛！是的，就是它！他长着一只鸟的眼睛，一只秃鹫的眼睛——一只淡蓝色的眼睛，上面蒙着一层薄膜。每当它落在我身上，我的血液就变冷；于是——非常缓慢地——我下定决心要取老人的性命，永远摆脱那只眼睛。

现在关键就在这里。你们以为我疯了。疯子什么都不懂。但你们真该看看我。你们真该看看我干活时是多么明智、多么小心！

在杀掉他之前的那整整一周里，我对老人从来没有那么和善过。而每天晚上，深更半夜，我转动他房门的锁，打开门——哦，是那么轻柔！然后，当我开出一条足够容下我脑袋的缝隙时，我放进一盏暗灯，全封闭着，不让一丝光亮透出，接着我把头探进去。我慢慢地、非常非常慢地移动脑袋，以免打扰老人睡觉。然后，当我的头完全进入房间后，我把提灯打开到刚好让一道细细的光线照到那只秃鹫眼睛上。

这样的做法我持续了七个漫长的夜晚——但我发现那只眼睛总是闭着；因此无法动手；因为对我来说，问题并不在于老人，而在于他的那只邪恶的眼睛。

第八天夜里，我开门时比平时更加小心。我的头已经探进去，正要打开提灯，这时我的手指在一块金属上滑了一下，发出声响。老人在床上坐起来，喊道：“谁在那儿？”

我一动不动，什么也没说。整整一个小时，我没有动一下肌肉。在那段时间里，我没有听到他躺下。他仍然坐在床上听着——就像我夜复一夜所做的那样。

接着我听到一种声音，我知道那是人类恐惧的声音。那是从灵魂深处涌出的低沉声音。我对这种声音再熟悉不过。多少个夜晚，深更半夜，当全世界都入睡时，它曾从我自己的胸腔深处涌上来。我说我熟悉它。

我知道老人感受到的是什么，并为他感到难过，尽管我在心里暗自好笑。我知道自第一声响动以来，他一直没有睡着，在床上翻来覆去。从那时起，他的恐惧就一直在不断加深。

我等了很久，一直没有听到他躺下，于是决定把提灯打开一条缝——一条非常非常小的缝。于是我打开了它。你无法想象那是多么小心、多么小心。终于，一道光线射了出来，正好落在那只秃鹫眼睛上。

那只眼睛睁着——睁得大大的——我看着它，心中渐渐愤怒起来。我看得很清楚——一片暗蓝，上面蒙着一层可怕的薄膜，令我不寒而栗；但我看不到老人面容或身体的任何其他部分。因为我把光线正好对准了那个该死的地方。

我不是告诉过你们，你们误认为是疯狂的东西，不过是一种过度敏感吗？现在，我耳边传来一种低沉、沉闷而急促的声音，就像手表裹在棉花里发出的声音一样。我也很熟悉那种声音。那是老人的心跳声。它使我更加愤怒。

但即使到这时，我依然一动不动。我几乎屏住了呼吸。我拿着提灯，一动不动。我努力让光线一直落在那只眼睛上。但心跳声越来越响。它一秒比一秒更快、更响。老人的恐惧一定到了极点！我说，那心跳声越来越响，每一刻都比上一刻更响！

此刻已是深夜，在这座老宅可怕的寂静中，这样一种奇怪的声音让我陷入无法控制的恐惧。然而，我又静静地站了几分钟。但那心跳声越来越响，越来越响！我想那颗心脏一定是要炸开了。

这时一种新的恐惧攫住了我——这声音会被邻居听到！老人的死期到了！我大喊一声，猛地掀开提灯，冲进了房间。

他叫了一声——只叫了一声。我毫不迟疑，把他按倒在地，把沉重的床推过去压在他身上。然后我笑了，发现事情已经做到这一步。

但是，好几分钟里，那颗心脏还在轻轻地跳动着。不过这并不让我担心；隔着墙，这声音不会被听到。终于，它停下了。老人死了。我移开床，检查了尸体。我把手按在他的心口上，按了好几分钟。没有动静。他彻底死了。他的那只眼睛不会再烦扰我了。

如果你仍认为我疯了，那么等我描述我为藏匿尸体所采取的明智步骤时，你就不会再这么想了。我动作很快，但悄无声息。首先，我把尸体肢解了。我砍下头、胳膊和腿。

然后我从地板上撬起三块木板，把他的身体部位放到地板下面。接着我把木板重新装好，装得如此严实，以致任何人的眼睛——甚至他的眼睛——都看不出任何异样。

没有什么需要冲刷的——没有任何痕迹——一点血迹都没有。我太聪明了，不会留下那些。一个大桶接住了所有——哈哈！

当我干完这些活时，已是凌晨四点钟。时钟敲响这个钟点的时候，街门传来敲门声。我轻快地走下去开门——因为我现在还有什么好怕的呢？进来三个人，他们自称是警察局的警官。夜里有个邻居听到了一声叫喊；这引起了犯罪的怀疑；有人向警察局报了案，警官们被派来搜查这栋房子。

我微笑了——因为我有什么好怕的呢？我说，那声叫喊是我自己在梦里发出的。我说，老人不在国内。我带着来访者把整栋房子都看了一遍。我叫他们搜查——仔细搜查。最后，我把他们领到了他的房间。我在那里搬来椅子，叫他们休息。我把自己的座位正好放在那个下面躺着受害者尸体的地方。

警官们很满意。我完全安心了。他们坐着，在我愉快地回答时，他们谈论着寻常的事情。但是，过了一会儿，我感到自己开始虚弱，希望他们离开。我的头很痛，耳朵里嗡嗡作响；但他们仍然坐在那里谈话。

那嗡嗡声变得更严重了。我更加随意地谈话，想消除这种感觉。但它持续不断，直到最后，我发现那声音不是在我的耳朵里。

我说得更多，声音也提高了。然而那声音反而增大了——我又能怎么办呢？那是一种低沉的、沉闷的、急促的声音，就像手表裹在棉花里发出的声音。我呼吸困难——然而那些警官却没有听见。我说得更快、更大声；但那声音反而增大了。我站起来，用很高的声调激烈地挥舞着手臂争论着愚蠢的事情。但那声音一直在增大。

他们为什么还不走？我迈着沉重的步伐在房间里走来走去，仿佛被那些人的话语激怒了——但那声音反而增大了。我能怎么办呢？我摇晃着椅子，在地板上推动它，但那声音不断地增大。它越来越响——越来越响——越来越响！而那些男人仍然愉快地说着话，微笑着。

他们不可能没听见吧？不，不！他们听见了！他们怀疑了！他们知道了！他们在拿我的恐惧开玩笑！我当时这么想，现在也这么想。但什么也比这种痛苦好受！我再也忍受不了那些微笑了！我觉得我必须喊出来，否则就会死去！而现在——又来了！更响了！更响了！更响了！

"恶棍们！"我喊道，"别再装了！我承认这件事是我干的！掀开地板吧！这里，就在这里！是他那颗可怕心脏的跳动声！"

你刚刚听到的是埃德加·爱伦·坡的短篇小说《泄密的心》。你的讲述人是谢普·奥尼尔。这个故事由雪莱·戈勒斯特改编。制作人是拉万·戴维斯。
